beginner: Strawberries grow best in loose, rich soil that drains well, like a sandy loam. Their roots are shallow, so they rot if the ground stays soggy. If your soil is heavy clay or puddles after rain, build a raised bed or a mounded row about 12 inches tall and plant into that. Mixing 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting gives the roots a good start.
seasoned: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with steady but not excessive moisture. The roots are shallow and fibrous, so they suffocate in soil that stays waterlogged for more than a day or two, and root rots follow. On heavy or slow-draining ground, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high so water drains away from the crowns. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost or aged organic matter into the bed before planting to lift organic matter above 3 percent.

beginner: Strawberries prefer soil on the slightly acidic side, roughly pH 5.6 to 6.5. A cheap test kit shows where you are. Garden sulfur lowers a too-high number; garden lime raises a too-low one. Both take a few months to take effect, so test and adjust the season before you plant.
seasoned: Aim for slightly acidic soil in the range of pH 5.6 to 6.5. Test the bed a season ahead so there is time to adjust: elemental sulfur brings a high reading down, and ground dolomitic limestone raises a low one. Both amendments take months to move the soil, so apply them well before the crowns go in.

beginner: Strawberries mainly need nitrogen, and when you feed depends on the type. The first year, give a little fertilizer two or three times spread across the season rather than one big dose. After that, the rule for June-bearing plants is simple: do not feed in spring, because it grows lots of leaves but not more berries, and the thick leaves trap dampness that causes mold. Feed them once instead, right after harvest when you cut the plants back. Day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all summer, get small amounts spread across the months instead. If your soil is sandy, feed smaller amounts more often.
seasoned: Strawberry feeding is nitrogen-driven and timed to the planting model. In the first year, apply a total of about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of actual nitrogen per 10 feet of row, split across the season: a small dose one to two weeks after planting, a second about a month later, and a third roughly two months after planting. On established June-bearing beds, do not feed in spring; spring nitrogen drives leaf growth, not fruit, and a dense canopy traps moisture and promotes gray mold. Instead, fertilize once at renovation, just after harvest, to build the flower buds for next year. Established day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all season, take the same total split into monthly doses through summer with an optional August feeding. On sandy soil, divide every rate into more frequent, lighter applications.

beginner: Your June-bearing strawberries are ready for their after-harvest cutback and feeding. Mow the old leaves, then give the plants a balanced fertilizer and water it in to help next year's berries.
seasoned: Time to renovate and feed your June-bearing strawberries. Mow the old leaves, narrow the row, then apply about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row and water it in to set next year's crop.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 16-16-16 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is a good all-purpose choice. Follow the label rate for the row length you are feeding, and water it in after spreading.
seasoned: A balanced analysis such as 16-16-16 works well. Rates are given as actual nitrogen per length of row, so divide the nitrogen you need by the decimal nitrogen fraction of your product: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet at renovation works out to roughly 2.5 to 3.75 ounces of 16-16-16 per 10-foot row.

beginner: A rough guide: feed a new bed lightly two or three times the first year. Feed an established June-bearing bed once, after harvest. Feed day-neutral or everbearing plants a little each month through summer. Use the label rate on your fertilizer for the length of your row.
seasoned: First year: about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row total, in two to three splits. Established June-bearers: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row, all at once at renovation. Day-neutral and everbearing: about 0.1 to 0.2 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet each month after spring growth begins, with an optional August dose.

beginner: The most important placement rule for strawberries is about what grew there before, not what you plant beside them. Do not put strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries grew recently. Those plants can leave a soil disease called Verticillium wilt behind, and it attacks strawberries too and stays in the soil for years. Also keep weeds out, since strawberries have shallow roots and lose out to weeds easily. The companion plants listed above are nice, low-risk neighbors, but they are garden tradition rather than a proven way to grow more fruit.
seasoned: The one firm rule for strawberry placement is rotation, not companionship: do not plant strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries have recently grown, because all of them host Verticillium wilt, a soilborne fungus that also attacks strawberries and lingers in the ground for years. Keep the same crops out of the bed for several years afterward. Beyond that, strawberries compete poorly with weeds because their roots are shallow, so the most valuable neighbor is bare, weed-free soil rather than any particular plant. The good-companion pairings above are traditional and low-risk, not documented yield boosters.

beginner: Beans are an easy, friendly neighbor for strawberries. They do not compete much and add a little nitrogen to the soil, though do not expect them to make your berries bigger.
seasoned: Bush beans bring nitrogen fixation to the strawberry bed. Working with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots, they pull atmospheric nitrogen into a plant-available form that lightly benefits strawberries as moderate feeders, and their upright, shallow habit does not compete much with low-running strawberry crowns. As with most legume pairings, the nitrogen mostly reaches neighbors as the bean roots break down, so treat it as gentle soil-building across the season rather than an immediate feed.

beginner: Lettuce fits nicely along the edge of a strawberry bed while the berries are still small, using space the strawberries are not using yet.
seasoned: Lettuce makes good use of the open space in a strawberry planting, especially in the first season before the strawberries fill in and run. It is shallow-rooted and quick, so it crops and clears before the strawberries need the room, and its low canopy helps shade soil and suppress weeds between crowns. A space-and-timing pairing rather than a pest or flavor one.

beginner: Borage is a herb with blue flowers that bees love. A few plants near your strawberries can bring in more bees, which helps the flowers turn into well-shaped berries.
seasoned: Borage is the traditional strawberry companion, and it is worth separating what it reliably does from what is folklore. Reliably: borage is a powerful bee magnet, and better pollinator visitation gives strawberries more complete fruit set and fewer misshapen berries, a real, mechanism-backed benefit. The older claim that borage directly improves strawberry flavor and yield through the soil is widely repeated but unsupported by controlled study, so lean on borage for pollination, not as a flavor additive.

beginner: Ragged holes eaten in the berries and leaves, with shiny slime trails. Worst in damp, mulchy beds and wet weather.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in ripe fruit and leaves, with slime trails, worst in damp, heavily mulched beds and wet weather.

beginner: Slugs, which hide in damp mulch and eat the soft ripe berries at night.
seasoned: Slugs, which shelter in deep or wet mulch and feed at night on soft ripe fruit.

beginner: Do not pile on thick straw in summer, keep the bed clean, and pick ripe berries quickly.
seasoned: Avoid deep straw mulch during the growing season, keep the bed tidy, and harvest ripe fruit promptly.

beginner: Start here: clear away damp hiding places, do not pile on thick straw mulch in summer, and keep the bed tidy so slugs have nowhere cool and wet to shelter by day. Pick ripe berries promptly so there is less soft fruit to draw them.
seasoned: Removing daytime shelter, avoiding deep summer mulch, and prompt harvest cut the slug population at its source; keep ripening fruit up off wet ground.

beginner: Hunt slugs after dark with a flashlight and pick them off, set board or beer traps for them to gather in, and ring the bed with copper strips they will not cross. Done regularly, handpicking alone can be very effective.
seasoned: Nighttime handpicking, board and beer-baited traps, and 2-inch copper barriers steadily lower numbers; empty and refresh traps every few days, and renew copper once it tarnishes.

beginner: If traps and cleanup are not enough, scatter iron phosphate slug bait on the soil, not on the plants. It is much safer around pets, kids, and wildlife than the old metaldehyde baits, though slugs take several days to die.
seasoned: Iron phosphate bait makes slugs stop feeding and is safer around pets and wildlife than metaldehyde; it works best alongside habitat removal, not alone, and takes several days to a week to kill.

beginner: Soft, sunken spots on ripening berries, with tiny maggots inside. It gets worse later in the season.
seasoned: Soft, collapsing spots on ripening and ripe fruit; tiny larvae feed inside berries. Populations build through the season, so later fruit is hit hardest.

beginner: A small fruit fly that lays eggs in the berries as they start to color, and the maggots eat the fruit from inside.
seasoned: A vinegar fly that lays eggs in coloring fruit; the larvae feed inside as the berry ripens.

beginner: Keep up with picking, never leave overripe berries on the plant, and use fine netting if the flies are bad.
seasoned: Harvest on a tight schedule, never leave overripe fruit on the plant, and exclude adults with fine netting where pressure is high.

beginner: Start here: pick all the ripe berries often and completely, and remove and destroy any overripe or damaged fruit. Overripe berries left on the plant are where this fly breeds, so tight, clean picking is your strongest everyday tool.
seasoned: Frequent, complete harvest and destroying culls removes the ripening fruit SWD breeds in; sanitation is the backbone, since populations build through the season and hit later fruit hardest.

beginner: Hang a cup of apple cider vinegar with a drop of dish soap near the berries to catch the flies. It tells you when they have arrived so you can time the other steps; it is a warning tool, not control.
seasoned: Vinegar traps checked weekly from before ripening detect adult arrival to time harvest and exclusion; monitoring, not control.

beginner: Cover the planting with very fine mesh, fine enough to stop no-see-ums, before the first berries start to color, and seal it to the ground. It physically keeps the flies off the fruit.
seasoned: Fine mesh, about 1 mm, installed before fruit colors and sealed at every edge down to the ground, excludes adult SWD; put it on too late and you trap flies inside with the fruit.

beginner: If pressure is high on a later crop, spinosad is the organic spray with the best track record on this fly, but it is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and mind the days-to-harvest on the label.
seasoned: Spinosad is the most effective organic material against SWD; rotate it to slow resistance, spray at dusk to spare bees, and observe the pre-harvest interval on a crop you pick continuously.

beginner: A last resort for heavy pressure only. It kills fast but hits bees and beneficials, and on a crop you pick every few days the days-to-harvest limit really matters, so read the label.
seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive, with a pre-harvest interval that is limiting on continuously harvested strawberries. Time it to dusk, off bloom.

beginner: Lumpy, dented berries with a pinched, seedy tip. Most common on day-neutral plants in summer.
seasoned: Catfaced fruit, dimpled and pinched at the tip with seedy, woody patches; most noticeable on day-neutrals in summer.

beginner: A small bug that feeds on the flowers and young fruit, which makes the berry tip grow lumpy.
seasoned: Lygus bugs feeding on developing flowers and fruit, which disrupts seed and berry development at the tip.

beginner: Pull broadleaf weeds near the bed, since the bugs breed on them, and keep the area tidy.
seasoned: Control broadleaf weeds that host lygus near the planting and keep the bed clean through the season.

beginner: Start here, and this is the main control: keep broadleaf weeds down in and around the bed, since that is where these bugs breed and shelter. Watch the flowers while fruiting so you catch a buildup early.
seasoned: Removing the broadleaf weeds that host lygus in and around the planting is the primary lever; scout flowers through fruiting, since the damage that catfaces fruit is done at bloom.

beginner: Minute pirate bugs, big-eyed bugs, and parasitic wasps feed on the young bugs, so avoid broad sprays that would kill them. Because lygus fly in from weeds and field edges, though, natural enemies only help so much on their own.
seasoned: Conserving natural enemies gives partial suppression, but lygus are mobile and reinvade from surrounding vegetation, so biological control is a supporting step, not a standalone fix; weed sanitation matters more.

beginner: Only if the bugs are ruining a lot of fruit and weeding has not been enough. A fast synthetic that also kills bees and beneficials, so keep it off flowers and treat it as a last resort.
seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive to the natural enemies above, with a label pre-harvest interval. Lygus are only moderately susceptible, so it does not substitute for weed control.

beginner: Groups of tiny soft bugs on new leaves and leaf undersides, leaving a sticky film. They can also spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and leaf undersides, with sticky honeydew and sometimes sooty mold; aphids can also transmit strawberry viruses.

beginner: Aphids, tiny bugs that suck plant juices and multiply fast on new leaves.
seasoned: Aphids feeding on plant sap, building up quickly on tender new growth.

beginner: Start with clean plants, and do not over-feed, since lots of soft new growth attracts aphids.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified plants to limit virus introduction, and avoid excess nitrogen that flushes soft, aphid-prone growth.

beginner: Start here: do not overfeed. Too much nitrogen pushes out soft new growth that aphids multiply on, so feed modestly. Starting with clean, certified plants also limits the viruses aphids can spread.
seasoned: Modest nitrogen keeps growth steady and less aphid-prone; clean certified stock limits virus introduction, since aphids also vector strawberry viruses.

beginner: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off the leaves, and most cannot climb back on. Do it early in the day so the leaves dry quickly.
seasoned: A forceful spray dislodges colonies from sturdy plants; spray early so foliage dries and disease is not encouraged.

beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps eat aphids and usually keep them in check for free. Protect them by not reaching for broad sprays.
seasoned: Resident ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae, and parasitic wasps hold aphids down; avoiding broad-spectrum sprays and managing the ants that tend them is what keeps them working.

beginner: For a heavy infestation, insecticidal soap kills the aphids you spray directly. It only works while wet, so coat them well, and it spares beneficials once dry.
seasoned: Contact soap smothers aphids with no residual, so coverage and repeat sprays matter; it spares dry-surface beneficials.

beginner: Neem oil is another low-residue option that coats and disrupts aphids. Do not spray it in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed plant, and spray at dusk to avoid wetting bees.
seasoned: Neem works by contact smothering and as an antifeedant and growth regulator; low toxicity to bees but, as a contact spray, apply at dusk. Avoid above 90°F or on stressed plants.

beginner: Rarely needed for aphids, and a last resort only. It kills fast but hits the ladybugs and other good bugs too, which can make aphids worse later, so keep it off flowers.
seasoned: Rescue-only and usually counterproductive on aphids, since it removes the natural enemies that regulate them and can trigger resurgence. Observe the label pre-harvest interval.

beginner: Leaves look speckled and bronzed, with fine webbing underneath. Worst in hot, dry, dusty weather, and bad cases weaken the plants.
seasoned: Fine stippling and bronzing of leaves with faint webbing on undersides, worst in hot, dry, dusty conditions; heavy infestations weaken plants and reduce yield.

beginner: Tiny mites under the leaves that multiply fast when it is hot and dry.
seasoned: Tiny mites that feed on the underside of leaves and multiply rapidly in hot, dry weather.

beginner: Keep plants watered in hot weather and avoid letting them get dusty and dry.
seasoned: Avoid drought stress and dusty conditions, and keep plants well watered in heat.

beginner: Start here: keep plants well watered, since spider mites flare on hot, dry, drought-stressed plants, and knock the mites back with a hard spray of water to the leaf undersides, which also raises the humidity they dislike. Keeping the bed from getting dusty helps too.
seasoned: Mites explode on drought-stressed, dusty plants, so steady watering is preventive; a forceful water spray to leaf undersides dislodges them and raises humidity. This foundation often keeps mites below the threshold that needs any spray.

beginner: Predatory mites and other tiny good bugs feed on spider mites and often control them on their own. Avoid broad sprays, including too much sulfur, that would kill these helpers.
seasoned: Predatory mites are the key natural enemy; conserve them by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays and sulfur, which set them back.

beginner: For a bad case, horticultural oil smothers the mites on contact. Cover the leaf undersides well, and do not spray in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed plant.
seasoned: Narrow-range oil knocks mites back by smothering; coverage of leaf undersides is everything. Avoid above 90°F, on stressed plants, or within 2 weeks of sulfur.

beginner: Neem oil is another contact option that coats and disrupts the mites. Same rules: thorough coverage, not in high heat, and spray at dusk to avoid bees.
seasoned: Neem gives partial mite control by contact and as a growth disruptor; repeat coverage is needed, and avoid high heat and stressed plants.

beginner: Sulfur is a last resort here. It does knock back spider mites, but it also harms the predatory mites that were helping you, so use it only if the softer steps have failed, and never in heat above 90°F.
seasoned: Sulfur is a protectant miticide but harms predatory mites, so it can trade a short knockdown for lost biological control; reserve it, keep a 2-week gap from any oil spray, and avoid above 90°F.

beginner: Leaf edges notched as if cut with pinking shears, and plants that wilt or collapse because grubs have eaten the roots and crown.
seasoned: Notched leaf margins from night-feeding adults, and stunted, wilting, or collapsing plants whose roots and crowns have been eaten by larvae.

beginner: Beetles whose adults chew the leaf edges at night and whose grubs eat the roots underground.
seasoned: Weevils whose adults notch leaves at night and whose larvae feed underground on roots and crowns.

beginner: Start new beds in a fresh spot, since the grubs build up in old beds, and use clean plants.
seasoned: Rotate to a fresh site when starting a new bed, since larvae build up in older plantings, and start with clean stock.

beginner: Start a new bed in a fresh spot away from old strawberry plantings, since the grubs build up in beds over the years. Begin with clean, healthy plants so you are not importing them.
seasoned: Siting a new planting away from older, infested beds starves the soil larvae, which build up over successive years; start with clean stock.

beginner: Pull and destroy badly infested plants in the fall, when the grubs are feeding on the roots and crown, so they do not carry over.
seasoned: Removing and destroying heavily infested plants in fall reduces the overwintering larval population.

beginner: On warm evenings the adult weevils come out to feed and notch the leaf edges. Go out with a flashlight and pick them off, since they cannot fly and are easy to catch by hand.
seasoned: The flightless adults feed at night; handpicking or shaking them onto a cloth after dark removes egg-laying females before the next generation of root-feeding larvae.

beginner: Beneficial nematodes are microscopic good worms you water into moist, warm soil. They hunt the grubs underground and are safe for people and pets.
seasoned: Entomopathogenic nematodes drenched into moist soil at roughly 60°F to 90°F infect the root-feeding larvae; time it to when larvae are present and keep the soil moist.

beginner: A last resort, and only against the adult beetles at night, since sprays cannot reach the grubs down in the soil. It hits bees and beneficials, so keep it off flowers and use it sparingly.
seasoned: Rescue-only and limited to adults, since foliar sprays do not reach soil larvae; broad-spectrum and disruptive, with a label pre-harvest interval. Nematodes are the better tool for the root-feeding stage.

beginner: Ripe berries pecked or half-eaten, often the best red ones taken right before you pick them.
seasoned: Pecked and partly eaten ripe berries, often the first fully colored fruit taken just before you would pick it.

beginner: Birds that go for the ripe red berries.
seasoned: Birds attracted to ripening red fruit.

beginner: Put netting on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have already found them.
seasoned: Net the planting before the first fruit ripens rather than after birds find it.

beginner: Shiny, moving, or noisy things like reflective tape and scare-eye balloons can frighten birds off for a while, but birds get used to them fast, so move them around and swap types at least weekly. On their own they do not reliably protect the fruit.
seasoned: Visual and noise deterrents reduce pressure but birds habituate; rotate device types and do not leave one combination up more than a week. Best paired with netting, not relied on alone.

beginner: The reliable fix is bird netting draped over hoops so it sits off the berries, with the edges tucked to the ground so birds cannot get underneath. Put it on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have found the patch.
seasoned: Netting on a hoop or PVC frame excludes birds; laid straight on the plants they still peck through it, so support it off the canopy, extend it to the ground, and tie the edges. Install before the first fruit colors.

beginner: Berries turn soft and rot, then grow a gray fuzz. It often starts where a berry touches the ground or another berry, and spreads quickly.
seasoned: A soft, tan rot of green and ripe fruit that quickly becomes a fuzzy gray mold, often starting where berries touch soil, mulch, or another berry. It spreads fast through a picked basket.

beginner: A mold that lives on old dead leaves and takes hold when it is wet while the plants are flowering and fruiting.
seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea, which overwinters on dead leaves and thrives when it rains during bloom and fruit development.

beginner: Do not feed June-bearing plants in spring, since extra leaves trap dampness. Water at the soil, give plants room to breathe, and pick ripe berries often.
seasoned: Avoid spring nitrogen on June-bearers, which thickens the canopy and traps moisture. Water at the base rather than overhead, space plants for airflow, and pick fruit promptly and often.

beginner: Start here: lay straw around and between the plants so the ripening berries sit up off the wet soil. Fruit that is not touching damp ground is far less likely to rot with gray mold.
seasoned: A good straw layer keeps fruit off wet soil and cuts rain splash, lowering Botrytis pressure; a foundational cultural step, though it reduces rather than eliminates rot.

beginner: Give plants room and water at the soil rather than overhead so the canopy dries quickly. Gray mold takes hold in damp, crowded, still foliage.
seasoned: Wide spacing and base watering shorten leaf and fruit wetness, denying Botrytis the sustained moisture it needs; an open canopy dries fast after rain.

beginner: Pick off and destroy moldy berries the moment you see them, since the mold spreads fast from one berry to the next, and clear away old dead leaves where it overwinters. Go easy on spring nitrogen, especially on June-bearers, since the extra soft leaves thicken the canopy and trap the dampness the mold loves.
seasoned: Remove infected fruit immediately and clean out old leaves at renovation and early spring; avoid spring nitrogen on June-bearers, which thickens the canopy and traps moisture. There is no home spray that cures it, so these cultural steps are the whole program.

beginner: Dark, sunken round spots on the berries. The disease can also rot the crown and runners, making plants wilt and die in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Dark, sunken, circular lesions on fruit; the fungus can also infect crowns and runners, causing wilting and plant death in warm, wet spells.

beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, wet, humid weather and splashes around in the rain.
seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi, favored by warm, humid, rainy conditions during fruit development and spread by splashing water.

beginner: Buy clean, certified plants, water at the base, and avoid spots where this disease has been a problem before.
seasoned: Start with certified disease-free plants, avoid overhead watering, and do not plant into ground with a recent history of the disease.

beginner: Start with clean, certified disease-free plants and, where anthracnose has been a problem, choose a resistant variety. Do not plant into ground with a recent history of the disease.
seasoned: Certified clean stock and resistant cultivars are the foundation, since the fungus arrives on infected transplants and persists in old sites; avoid replanting into a recent-history bed.

beginner: Lay straw mulch to keep berries off the soil and cut down on rain splashing spores up onto the fruit, which is how this disease spreads.
seasoned: Mulch reduces the rain and irrigation splash that disperses Colletotrichum spores; water at the base rather than overhead.

beginner: Pull off and destroy diseased berries and plants promptly, and give plants room so the canopy dries. Watering at the soil instead of overhead keeps spores from splashing around.
seasoned: Prompt removal of diseased fruit and plants lowers inoculum; base watering and airflow limit the warm, wet, splashing conditions the fungus needs.

beginner: If the cultural steps are not holding in a warm, wet season, a copper spray can protect healthy fruit, but it must go on before infection and cannot cure berries already rotting. Copper is toxic to fish and builds up in the soil, so use it sparingly.
seasoned: Fixed copper is a protectant only, applied before infection during warm wet spells; it will not cure established rot. Copper accumulates in soil and harms aquatic life, so limit repeat use.

beginner: Leaf edges curl upward and turn purple, with a white dusty coating. In some varieties the berries taste bitter.
seasoned: Upward cupping and purpling of leaf edges with a white powdery film; in some cultivars infected fruit tastes bitter.

beginner: A fungus that spreads when the air is humid but the leaves are dry.
seasoned: A fungus that, unlike most strawberry diseases, spreads in dry conditions with high humidity and moderate temperatures.

beginner: Give plants room, keep them from getting crowded, and choose mildew-resistant varieties.
seasoned: Space plants well, avoid dense canopies, and select tolerant cultivars.

beginner: The easiest fix is to grow a mildew-resistant variety, especially if it keeps coming back or if it makes your berries taste bitter.
seasoned: Cultivar resistance varies widely and is the lowest-effort durable control; worth choosing where mildew recurs, since some cultivars also develop off-flavored fruit.

beginner: Give plants room and keep the canopy from getting crowded. Unlike most strawberry diseases, mildew spreads when the air is humid even if the leaves stay dry, so airflow still helps. Pick off the worst-affected leaves.
seasoned: Wide spacing and an open canopy lower the humidity mildew favors, since it spreads in dry-leaf, high-humidity conditions; remove badly affected leaves.

beginner: If mildew is heavy, sulfur is the organic spray, applied before it takes hold. Some strawberry varieties are sensitive to it, so test a few plants first, and never spray in heat above 90°F.
seasoned: Sulfur is a protectant for powdery mildew, but some strawberry cultivars are sulfur-sensitive, so spot-test first; avoid above 90°F and within 2 weeks of oil, and note it harms predatory mites.

beginner: Plants are stunted and wilt, then collapse in spring. If you cut a root open, the center is reddish-brown. It is worst in heavy, wet soil that drains poorly.
seasoned: Stunted, wilting plants that collapse in spring; roots are rotted and, when sliced lengthwise, show a reddish-brown core. Worst in heavy, wet, poorly drained soil.

beginner: A soil fungus that builds up in cold, soggy ground and stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora fungi that thrive in cold, saturated soils and persist for years.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds, buy certified plants, and pick resistant varieties if your ground stays wet.
seasoned: Plant only in well-drained soil or raised beds, start with certified plants, and choose red-stele-resistant cultivars on wet sites.

beginner: This is a soilborne rot with no home cure, so prevention is everything. On wet ground, the single most important choice is a red-stele-resistant variety, and always start with certified disease-free plants.
seasoned: Red-stele-resistant cultivars are the primary control for a soilborne Phytophthora that persists for years and cannot be cured; pair with certified clean stock.

beginner: Plant only in well-drained soil or raised beds, since this rot thrives in cold, soggy ground, and do not replant strawberries into a bed where it has struck, because the fungus lingers in the soil for years. Pull and destroy any collapsing plants.
seasoned: Improve drainage with raised beds and rotate off infested ground for years, since the pathogen is soilborne and persistent; there is no chemical rescue, so remove and destroy affected plants. Drainage, a fresh well-drained site, and resistant varieties are the whole game.

beginner: The outer leaves wilt, dry at the edges, and flop down while the middle leaves stay up. Plants are stunted and may die, often as the berries are forming.
seasoned: Outer leaves wilt, dry at the margins, and collapse while inner leaves may stay upright; plants are stunted and may die. Symptoms often appear as fruit load increases.

beginner: A soil fungus that also attacks tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, and other berries, and stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Verticillium, which also infects tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, and brambles and persists in soil for years.

beginner: Do not plant strawberries where you recently grew tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or other berries, and start with certified clean plants.
seasoned: Do not plant strawberries after or near tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, and start with certified disease-free stock on a clean site.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant wilts, so it comes down to variety and site. Choose a verticillium-resistant strawberry variety and start with certified disease-free plants.
seasoned: Resistant cultivars and certified clean stock are the primary controls for a soilborne fungus with no rescue treatment; variety choice does much of the work.

beginner: Do not plant strawberries where you recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, since verticillium builds up on all of them and lingers in the soil for years. Pick a clean site with no recent history.
seasoned: The fungus infects many hosts, including tomato, pepper, eggplant, potato, and brambles, and persists for years, so rotate onto ground clear of those crops; site choice is the main lever.

beginner: Pull and destroy plants as they wilt, so they do not add to what is in the soil, and keep the bed clean.
seasoned: Removing affected plants limits soil buildup; there is no spray, so sanitation supports the rotation and variety program rather than curing anything.

beginner: Give strawberries about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week while they are growing. Water more often in hot weather or sandy soil, and keep new plants well watered since their roots are still small.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week through the growing season, adjusted for vigor, growth stage, soil, and weather. On sandy soil and in heat, water more often and more lightly. Newly set plants have undeveloped roots and stress easily, so irrigate several times a week until established.

beginner: Water enough to wet the soil about 6 inches to a foot deep, so the roots stay moist but never soggy. Strawberry roots are shallow and rot if they sit in water, so do not overdo it.

seasoned: Cover blooming plants when a late frost threatens; open strawberry flowers are killed at right around freezing, and the giveaway is a blackened center in the flower the next morning. A row cover or even a sheet over the bed saves that first set.

seasoned: Keep water steady and keep pollinators welcome through bloom. Each berry is built from many fertilized seeds on the flower, so poor pollination is what gives you small, lopsided, misshapen fruit even when the plant looks healthy.

beginner: Pick the fully red berries every couple of days, snapping the stem instead of pulling. Strawberries do not get sweeter after picking, so let them ripen on the plant.
seasoned: Pick fully red, ripe berries every two to three days, pinching the stem rather than tugging the fruit. Replace the bed with fresh nursery stock every two to three years as heat and disease pressure accumulate. Bees still help a lot: a flower that gets plenty of bee visits makes a big, even berry, while one that does not can make a small or lumpy one. beginner: In the first year, June-bearing strawberries do best if you pinch off all their flowers as they appear. It feels wrong to remove flowers, but it lets the plant build strong roots and send out runners that fill the bed, so you get a big crop the next year instead of a few berries now. Let those runners take root to fill in the row. Day-neutral and everbearing plants only need their flowers pinched for the first month or so, and then you let them fruit.
seasoned: For June-bearers, pinch off every flower the entire first season so the plant pours its energy into roots, crown, and runners instead of a small early crop; the payoff is a strong matted row and a full harvest in year two. Let the early runners root in the row to build the bed, and sweep stray runners back into the row before they root in the aisles. Day-neutral and everbearing plants are pinched only for the first four to six weeks after planting, then allowed to fruit the same season.

beginner: Strawberries like loose, rich soil that drains well. Their roots are shallow and rot in soggy ground, so if your soil is heavy clay or puddles after rain, build a raised bed or mound about 12 inches tall and plant into that. Mix in an inch or two of compost before planting. Strawberries prefer slightly acidic soil, so test it the season before and adjust if needed. Do not plant where tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or other berries grew recently, because they leave behind a soil disease that attacks strawberries.
seasoned: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam rich in organic matter. Because the roots are shallow and rot in waterlogged soil, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high on heavy or slow-draining ground. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting and adjust pH to 5.6 to 6.5 a season ahead, since sulfur or lime take months to act. Avoid ground that recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, which leave Verticillium wilt in the soil.

beginner: Renovation is a once-a-year tidy-up for June-bearing strawberries, done a week or two after the last berries are picked. Mow or cut the old leaves down to about 2 inches above the crowns (the thick stems at soil level), being careful not to cut into the crowns. Rake away the cut leaves, narrow the row back to about a hand's width by removing plants from the edges, then feed and water so the plants put out fresh leaves before winter. Skip this for day-neutral and everbearing types, since they are still making fruit in late summer.
seasoned: Renovation applies to June-bearing matted rows. Do it within a week or two of picking the final berries, while the plants still have time to regrow before fall. Mow or shear the old leaves to roughly 2 inches above the crowns without cutting into the crowns themselves, rake out the debris to cut next spring's fruit rot, narrow the row back to about 10 to 12 inches by tilling or hoeing the edges, then fertilize and water to push fresh leaf and runner growth. Leave day-neutral and everbearing plants alone, since they are still fruiting in late summer.

beginner: There are three kinds of strawberries, and picking the right one matters more than picking a fancy variety. June-bearing types give you one big harvest over about four weeks in late spring or early summer, perfect if you want a pile of berries at once for jam or the freezer. They spread by sending out runners that fill in a wide row, and they give their first real crop the year after you plant them. Day-neutral types fruit a little at a time from late spring all the way to fall, give berries the first year, and stay compact, so they are the best choice for pots and small raised beds. Everbearing types fall in between, with one crop in early summer and another in late summer. This guide is built around the June-bearing kind grown in a wide row, since that is how most home gardeners grow strawberries, and it points out along the way where day-neutrals are handled differently. In mild coastal areas with gentle winters, day-neutral plants can give berries through much of the year, and gardeners there often plant fresh ones each year instead of keeping a bed for years.
seasoned: Strawberries come in three types, and the choice shapes your whole season. June-bearing cultivars set flower buds in the short days of fall and deliver one concentrated crop over about four weeks in late spring or early summer; they throw the most runners, so they suit a matted row and give a large flush ideal for freezing and jam. Their first real crop comes the season after planting. Day-neutral cultivars flower regardless of day length whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90°F, so they fruit from late spring through fall, bear in their first season, and throw few runners, which makes them the pick for containers, raised beds, and a steady supply of fresh berries. Everbearing cultivars give two lighter crops, one in early summer and one in late summer, and are generally less productive than day-neutrals. This guide follows the June-bearing matted-row model because it is the backbone of US backyard strawberry growing; the day-neutral notes throughout tell you where the care diverges. In mild-winter coastal regions, day-neutral plantings can fruit across much of the year and are often grown as a fall-set annual rather than a long-lived bed, which is why the warm-region notes treat them differently from the cold-region matted row.
